To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the scaling of the number of heads to the size of the heads in existing architectures gives rise  to the large embedding requirement and we propose a new method to train models with smaller embedding dimension, while retaining the performance.

(1) we identify the scaling between the size of the heads and the number of heads in attention models as a factor that contributes to the large embedding dimension requirement, and (2) we propose a new approach to setting the projection size in heads that allows us train models with a smaller embedding dimension.

(1) the scaling between the size of the embedding dimension and the number of attention heads is not necessary, and (2) we can achieve the same level of performance with a much smaller embedding dimension by setting a different scaling between the size and number of attention heads.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following two questions: (1) Why do we need large embedding dimension for the transformer architecture?
two main questions: 1) Why are the existing attention based models so sensitive to the embedding dimension?
the following questions: (1) How can we train smaller models without sacrificing performance? (2) What is the role of the number of attention heads and the embedding size?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we can achieve the same performance as existing models with a smaller model size by using the proposed multi-head attention model.
our proposed models are able to achieve the same performance as the existing models while using 2x smaller embedding dimension, and are 2x faster to train.
our proposed method is able to reduce the embedding dimension of a Transformer architecture by half, without sacrificing the model performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a new attention architecture which allows for a more compact embedding dimension while maintaining the performance.
, we present an alternative to the existing scaling between the number and the size of attention heads in the multi-head attention mechanism.
we present a new approach for setting projection sizes in attention heads which enables us to train models of smaller size with comparable performance to the larger ones.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the attention heads in Transformer architectures should not be scaled proportionally to the embedding size.
the existing scaling between the number and the projection size of attention heads is sub-optimal.
, with a careful choice of parameters, one can achieve a significant reduction in the model size without compromising the quality of the predictions.
